Subject: what I found on the Q2 estimates

Hi Payal,

You asked why the Q2 launch was late again, so I went through the tracker. When I made the estimates, I put a big cushion on every task, so each one had ten days for what is really four days of work. The team relaxed. Nobody started early, and most tasks were touched for the first time in the last two days before their dates. Testing came at the very end and squeezed everything. The days I padded never turned into spare days. I believed the padding would keep everyone calm, but calm turned into slow.

Can we talk on Monday about what a better estimate could look like?

Gurpreet

qa.q: How many days did each task get for what was really four days of work?
qa.a: Each task had ten days for what is really four days of work.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet expect the padding to do?
qa.a: Gurpreet expected the padding to keep everyone calm, but the calm turned into slowness.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet do instead of padding every task?
qa.a: Gurpreet could keep honest estimates for each task and hold one shared cushion near the end for real delays, so tasks do not stretch to fill their days.

qa.q: How might Payal feel on reading this email?
qa.a: Payal, who asked why the launch was late again, may feel relieved to get a clear answer, and perhaps frustrated that the launch slipped.

grounding: Shows a heavy cushion added to every estimate, so the team relaxes and still finishes at the last minute.

passage:
Zainab, you asked on the podcast about the worst planning habit I've seen. Let Afreen tell you about a team I worked on two years ago.
Our lead, a really kind person, padded every estimate. If a task needed two days, she wrote five. If a report needed a week, she wrote three. She said, "Better safe than sorry."
And for a while it felt great. Nobody was stressed. But here's what happened. With five days for a two-day job, people started on day four. Meetings got longer. Emails piled up. Everyone relaxed, because the deadline looked so far away.
Then everything finished on the last possible afternoon anyway, in a rush, with the same late nights as before.
All that extra time never turned into anything saved. It just filled up. By the end of the year, we were slower than the team next door, which padded nothing.

qa.q: How many days did the lead write for a two-day task?
qa.a: If a task needed two days, she wrote five.

qa.q: How might the team have felt in the early days of each task?
qa.a: They probably felt calm and unhurried, since the deadline seemed far away, which is why they started late.

qa.q: What would you change first in how the lead planned?
qa.a: Give realistic estimates for each task and keep one shared buffer at the end, used only for real delays, so the time isn't quietly used up.

qa.q: How might the team next door have seen Afreen's team?
qa.a: They may have seen a team with lots of time on paper that still rushed at the end, and finished slower overall.

grounding: It shows a colleague padding every estimate so the team relaxes and still finishes at the last minute, with the padding never turning into saved time.

I'm Amandeep. I sit across from Imran in the marketing team, and I've watched his estimates for a year.
Every task he quotes has a huge cushion. A two-page brochure: "Give me two weeks." A client email: "By Friday," on a Monday. The manager usually agrees, because Imran is never late.
But here's what I see from my desk. For the first week and a half of those two weeks, the brochure file doesn't open. He helps others, takes long lunches, answers messages. Then on the last two days he's hunched over it till nine at night, exactly like people with tight deadlines.
Last month the manager asked why our team is slower than the design team, which quotes shorter times. Nobody had a clear answer.
I don't know if Imran feels stressed in those last two days. He always says it's fine. But the extra time never seems to be there when he needs it.

qa.q: How long does Imran quote for a two-page brochure?
What might Imran being hunched over the file till nine at night suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels pressured and rushed at the end, even though he says it's fine, though Amandeep can't be sure.

qa.q: What could the team try instead of padding every estimate?
qa.a: Estimate each task honestly and keep one shared buffer for the whole project, so extra time is saved for real delays.

qa.q: How might the manager see the team's slowness?
qa.a: The manager is puzzled, since Imran is never late but the team is slower than the design team, and no one can explain why.

grounding: It shows a colleague adding a large buffer to every estimate, so work expands to fill it and still ends in a last-minute rush.
